pos: n. (Anthony Tuckney, 1599–1670, Westminster divine, Master of Emmanuel and of St John's, Cambridge)
etymology: Greek Antonios through Latin, of uncertain sense; English Tuckney, a place-name surname of Lincolnshire.
biblical_def: Anthony Tuckney succeeded John Cotton at Boston in Lincolnshire, sat in the Westminster Assembly, became Master of Emmanuel College and then of St John's, Cambridge, and Regius Professor of Divinity; he is credited with a large share in the drafting of the Shorter Catechism. He was ejected from his chair at the Restoration. His most instructive remains are the letters he exchanged with Benjamin Whichcote, his former pupil and by then the leading figure among the Cambridge divines who were beginning to exalt reason and natural light as the measure of religion. Tuckney wrote to him with real affection and absolute firmness: that reason is God's gift and not His rival, that the light of nature does not supply the gospel, and that a divinity which blushes at the doctrine of sin and of free grace will not long keep Christ. The dictionary reckons those letters one of the clearest early warnings against latitudinarian religion, written before anyone had a name for it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines latitudinarian as one who indulges a freedom in thinking beyond the limits of orthodoxy, and catechism as instruction by question and answer.
webster_full: LATITUDINA'RIAN, n. One who is moderate in his notions, or not restrained by precise settled limits in religion.
CAT'ECHISM, n. A form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.
RE'GIUS, a. Royal; as the Regius Professor, a chair founded by the sovereign.
REA'SON, n. A faculty of the mind by which it distinguishes truth from falsehood.
scriptures: But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned.
Rom 1:21
Because that, when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened.
Jer 17:9
The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?
For after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe.
corruption_summary: His letters to Whichcote are an early warning against a divinity that makes reason and natural light the measure.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is latitudinarianism: the elevation of reason and the light of nature to the place of judge over revelation, with a corresponding embarrassment at the doctrines of original sin, election and particular grace. It began among able and devout men at Cambridge in the 1650s, and within two generations it had produced an English divinity that could speak of virtue at length and of the cross hardly at all. Tuckney saw the direction while Whichcote was still only genial.

The standard is the natural man's incapacity and God's chosen means. “But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him” (1Co 2:14). What men do with the light they have is stated: “when they knew God, they glorified him not as God” (Rom 1:21). The heart is not a reliable instrument: “The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?” (Jer 17:9). And the means God appointed is deliberately not philosophy — “it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe” (1Co 1:21).

pos: n. (Thomas Coleman, 1598–1646, Westminster divine, Hebraist, and the Assembly's leading Erastian)
etymology: Aramaic Te'oma through Greek Thomas, a twin; English Coleman, a charcoal burner.
biblical_def: Thomas Coleman was a Lincolnshire rector so accomplished in Hebrew that the Assembly called him Rabbi Coleman, and he was the most articulate spokesman in that body for the Erastian position: that the power of church censures, and in particular of excommunication, belongs properly to the Christian magistrate and not to a separate ecclesiastical court. He argued it in sermons before Parliament and in print against George Gillespie, and the Assembly rejected it. The dictionary names the error and keeps the man. Coleman was a serious exegete who held that the New Testament gives elders the ministry of the word and leaves the sword, including the sword of discipline, with the state; his motive was a horror of clerical tyranny, which is a real danger. He was nonetheless wrong, and the texts he had to explain away are the ones the Assembly put in the Confession.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Erastian as a follower of Erastus, who denied the church's power of excommunication, and censure as judicial sentence of a church.
webster_full: ERAS'TIAN, n. A follower of Erastus, who maintained that the church has no power of censure or excommunication independent of the civil magistrate.
CEN'SURE, n. The act of blaming or finding fault; judicial sentence; the spiritual punishment inflicted by a church.
EXCOMMUNICA'TION, n. The act of ejecting from the communion of the church.
RAB'BI, n. A title given by the Jews to their doctors and teachers of the law.
scriptures: And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican.
For what have I to do to judge them also that are without? do not ye judge them that are within?
Jesus answered, My kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight, that I should not be delivered to the Jews: but now is my kingdom not from hence.
And I will give unto thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth shall be bound in heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.
corruption_summary: The Assembly's leading Erastian, rejected on the point and honoured for his Hebrew.
corruption_paragraphs: The error to name is Erastianism: the doctrine that the church possesses no power of discipline distinct from the civil magistrate's, so that excommunication is either the state's act or no act at all. Its appeal is real, since clerical courts have often been tyrannical, and the English experience of the High Commission made the argument popular. Its cost is that the keys our Lord gave to His church are handed to Caesar, and a church which cannot exclude an impenitent man cannot keep a table.

The standard is where Christ lodged the authority. The last court in His procedure is the congregation: “tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican” (Mat 18:17). Paul distinguishes the two jurisdictions plainly: “For what have I to do to judge them also that are without? do not ye judge them that are within?” (1Co 5:12). The kingdom itself is of another order — “My kingdom is not of this world” (Joh 18:36) — and the keys were given to the church: “I will give unto thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Mat 16:19).

pos: n. (Francis Cheynell, 1608–1665, Westminster divine and opponent of Socinianism)
etymology: Latin Franciscus, a Frenchman, free; English Cheynell, from Old French chenel, an oak grove.
biblical_def: Francis Cheynell sat in the Westminster Assembly, was made President of St John's College, Oxford, and wrote the fullest English warning of his generation against Socinianism, tracing its rise in Poland, its spread into the Netherlands and England, and the particular English books that were carrying it. He also wrote an account of the death of William Chillingworth, which does him no credit as a man: he treated a dying opponent harshly and published the fact. The dictionary records both. Cheynell was right about the danger and ugly in his manner, and these are two separate judgments. His book correctly identified the Socinian denial of Christ's eternal Godhead and of His satisfaction as the coming English heresy, and the eighteenth century proved him right as congregation after congregation of English Presbyterians slid first into Arianism and then into open Unitarianism.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Socinian as one who denies the divinity and atonement of Christ, and satisfaction as that which atones for a wrong.
webster_full: SOCIN'IAN, n. One of the followers of Socinus, who denied the divinity of Christ and the doctrine of satisfaction for sin.
SATISFAC'TION, n. That which satisfies; atonement for a crime; indemnification for an injury.
PRES'IDENT, n. An officer appointed to preside over a college or society.
HER'ESY, n. A fundamental error in religion.
scriptures: Joh 1:1
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
Rom 3:25
Whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness for the remission of sins that are past, through the forbearance of God;
And he is the propitiation for our sins: and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world.
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
corruption_summary: He warned England of Socinianism and was proved right, and he treated a dying opponent badly.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is Socinianism, which denies the eternal Godhead of the Son and the propitiatory satisfaction He made, reducing the cross to an example and salvation to obedient imitation. Cheynell traced it from Poland into England and named its carriers. He was not imagining a threat: the English Presbyterian congregations of the next century went over to Arianism and then Unitarianism in large numbers, and their meeting houses are the monument.

The standard is the Godhead of the Son and the nature of His death. “and the Word was God” (Joh 1:1). The cross is a propitiation that satisfies God's justice: Christ was set forth “to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness” (Rom 3:25). “And he is the propitiation for our sins” (1Jo 2:2). And the purchase price is named with a deliberate boldness: the church of God, “which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28).

Greek hilasmos (G2434) — a propitiation, an atoning sacrifice; 1 John 2:2.

Greek logos (G3056) — word, the Son as God's self-expression; John 1:1.
Greek dikaiosune (G1343) — righteousness, justice; Romans 3:25.

“a propitiation through faith in his blood” (Rom 3:25) — the satisfaction it reduces to an example.
“which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28) — a warning the next century vindicated.

pos: n. (Jeremiah Whitaker, 1599–1654, Westminster divine, long afflicted and known for patience)
etymology: Hebrew Yirmeyahu, the LORD exalts; English Whitaker, dweller at the white field.
biblical_def: Jeremiah Whitaker was rector of Stretton in Rutland and then of St Mary Magdalen, Bermondsey, a member of the Westminster Assembly and for a time its prolocutor in Dr Twisse's absence. The last years of his life were spent in great pain from the stone, borne, by every account his friends left, with a patience that became the thing he was chiefly remembered for; Simeon Ashe's funeral sermon for him dwells on it at length. He preached before Parliament and left little in print. The dictionary gives him an entry for his sickbed. The Westminster Assembly is remembered for its documents, and the documents were produced by men who were also bearing the ordinary and extraordinary afflictions of the body; what a divine does in a year of pain is as much a part of his testimony as what he writes in a committee, and in Whitaker's case it was the better part.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines patience as the suffering of afflictions with a calm temper, and infirmity as an unsound state of the body.
webster_full: PA'TIENCE, n. The suffering of afflictions, pain, toil, calamity or provocation with a calm, unruffled temper; endurance without murmuring.
INFIRM'ITY, n. An unsound or unhealthy state of the body; weakness; feebleness.
PROLO'CUTOR, n. The chairman or speaker of a convocation or assembly.
AFFLIC'TION, n. The state of being afflicted; a state of pain, distress or grief.
scriptures: Job 2:10
But he said unto her, Thou speakest as one of the foolish women speaketh. What? shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil? In all this did not Job sin with his lips.

And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.
Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby.
Rom 5:3
And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience;
corruption_summary: A Westminster divine whose long illness, borne patiently, became his best-remembered testimony.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern treatment of suffering as an interruption of a life rather than a part of it, so that a Christian in pain assumes his usefulness is suspended until he is well. Whitaker's friends thought his most convincing years were the painful ones.

The principle to recover is that affliction is given, is to be received from God's hand, and yields fruit. Job's question is the pattern: “shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?” (Job 2:10). The answer to Paul's prayer was not removal: “My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness” (2Co 12:9). Chastening is not pleasant and it is productive — “nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness” (Heb 12:11) — and the apostle can therefore say “we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience” (Rom 5:3).

roots_lines: Greek hupomone (G5281) — patient endurance, steadfastness; Romans 5:3.
Greek astheneia (G769) — weakness, infirmity, sickness; 2 Corinthians 12:9.
Greek teleo (G5055) — to finish, to make perfect; 2 Corinthians 12:9.
Greek paideia (G3809) — chastening, instruction by discipline; Hebrews 12:11.
Hebrew ra (H7451) — evil, adversity, calamity; Job 2:10.
usage: “shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?” (Job 2:10) — years of the stone.
“My grace is sufficient for thee” (2Co 12:9) — prolocutor of the Assembly in Twisse's absence.
“it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness” (Heb 12:11) — the thing his friends remembered first.

pos: n. (John Ley, 1583–1662, Westminster divine, sub-dean of Chester and one of the Assembly's annotators)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan through Latin Johannes, the LORD is gracious; English Ley, from Old English leah, a clearing, a meadow.
biblical_def: John Ley was a Cheshire minister, sub-dean of Chester cathedral, a member of the Westminster Assembly, and one of the divines who produced the Annotations upon all the books of the Old and New Testament — the large commentary commissioned by Parliament and published in the 1640s, in which a team of ministers wrote short notes on every chapter so that English families had a help beside the Authorized Version. He also wrote on the sabbath and on the keeping of parish registers. The dictionary names the Annotations as the work that matters. It was a committee commentary, written quickly, uneven in places, and in nearly every English Protestant household of substance for a century; its notes shaped how ordinary Englishmen read their Bibles more than any single divine's treatise did. Collective, unglamorous, useful work of that kind is the ordinary way the church's learning reaches the pew.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines annotation as a remark or note upon an author, and register as a book in which entries are recorded.
webster_full: ANNOTA'TION, n. A remark, note or commentary on some passage of a book.
REG'ISTER, n. A book in which are recorded the names of persons, or the transactions of a body.
SUB'DEAN, n. The deputy or substitute of a dean; an under dean.
COM'MENTARY, n. A series of comments or annotations; an exposition of a book.
scriptures: Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
Act 8:31
And he said, How can I, except some man should guide me? And he desired Philip that he would come up and sit with him.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.
corruption_summary: One of the annotators whose parliamentary commentary sat beside the Authorized Version in English households.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a suspicion of study notes as a crutch that stands between the reader and the text. Notes can be abused that way; the English experience was the opposite. Families who had the Annotations read more of the Bible, not less, because the hard chapters stopped stopping them.

The principle to recover is that God gives teachers precisely so that readers understand, and that asking for help is not weakness. The Levites “gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8). The Ethiopian's answer to Philip states the ordinary case: “How can I, except some man should guide me?” (Act 8:31). All scripture is profitable for teaching — “profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness” (2Ti 3:16) — and counsel in numbers is safety: “in the multitude of counsellors there is safety” (Pro 11:14).

Greek ophelimos (G5624) — profitable, useful; 2 Timothy 3:16.
Hebrew yaats (H3289) — to counsel, to advise; Proverbs 11:14.

“How can I, except some man should guide me?” (Act 8:31) — notes on every chapter for families.
“in the multitude of counsellors there is safety” (Pro 11:14) — a committee commentary, uneven and indispensable.

pos: n. (George Walker, c. 1581–1651, Westminster divine and London minister, writer on the covenants)
etymology: Greek Georgios, a husbandman; English Walker, a fuller of cloth.
biblical_def: George Walker was rector of St John the Evangelist in Watling Street, London, for nearly forty years, a member of the Westminster Assembly, and a controversialist on the article of justification. His long dispute with Anthony Wotton turned on whether Christ's righteousness is imputed to the believer in the proper sense or whether faith itself is counted as righteousness, and Walker contended for imputation; the quarrel was bitter and Walker was for a time out of favour with his brethren over the manner of it. He also wrote on the sabbath and on the covenants, distinguishing the covenant of works made with Adam from the covenant of grace. The dictionary follows him on the doctrine. Imputation is the article on which the Reformation's doctrine of justification stands or falls: either a righteousness not our own is reckoned to us, or we are at last justified by something in ourselves, however it is named.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines impute as to charge or attribute to, and covenant as a mutual agreement or compact.
webster_full: IMPU'TE, v.t. To charge; to attribute; to set to the account of; to attribute to another what properly belongs to the person charged.
COV'ENANT, n. A mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons, to do or to forbear some act.
RIGHT'EOUSNESS, n. The quality or state of being right; conformity of heart and life to the divine law.
CONTROVER'SY, n. Dispute; debate; agitation of contrary opinions.
scriptures: Rom 4:5
But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness.
Rom 4:6
Even as David also describeth the blessedness of the man, unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works,
For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.
Gen 17:7
And I will establish my covenant between me and thee and thy seed after thee in their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God unto thee, and to thy seed after thee.
corruption_summary: He contended for the imputation of Christ's righteousness against making faith itself our righteousness.
corruption_paragraphs: The error to name is the subtle one Walker fought: that in justification God counts the act of faith as our righteousness, rather than reckoning to us the righteousness of Christ which faith receives. The difference looks small and it decides everything. If faith is the righteousness, then a work of mine, albeit a gracious one, is the ground of my acceptance; if Christ's obedience is the righteousness and faith only the empty hand, then the ground is wholly outside me and cannot be shaken by my weakness.

The standard is Paul's language of reckoning. “But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness” (Rom 4:5) — counted for, as the instrument, and the next verse makes the imputation explicit: God “imputeth righteousness without works” (Rom 4:6). The exchange is stated in full at Corinth: “For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him” (2Co 5:21). And the covenant in which all this is held is everlasting — “an everlasting covenant, to be a God unto thee, and to thy seed after thee” (Gen 17:7).

pos: n. (Henry Scudder, d. 1652, Westminster divine, author of The Christian's Daily Walk)
etymology: Germanic Heinrich, home-ruler; English Scudder, from scud, to run or move quickly.
biblical_def: Henry Scudder was minister at Collingbourne Ducis in Wiltshire and then at Colyton, a member of the Westminster Assembly, and the author of The Christian's Daily Walk in Holy Security and Peace — a practical handbook on how a believer orders a day: rising, prayer, work, speech, company, meals, temptation, and lying down again. It went through edition after edition in English, was translated into Dutch and German, and was recommended by John Owen and Richard Baxter alike. The dictionary names it the best sort of practical divinity. Scudder does not offer a method for producing holiness; he assumes the gospel, assumes a justified man, and then answers the question such a man actually asks, which is what to do between breakfast and bed. Doctrine that never reaches the hours of the day has not been believed yet, and books like this one are how the Puritans made sure theirs did.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines walk as the manner of living, course of life, and security as freedom from fear or apprehension of danger.
webster_full: WALK, n. Manner of walking; gait; step; course of life or conduct; deportment.
SECU'RITY, n. Freedom from fear or apprehension; confidence of safety; that which secures.
PRAC'TICAL, a. Pertaining to practice or action; capable of being turned to use.
CLOS'ET, n. A small room or apartment for retirement; any place of privacy, as for prayer.
scriptures: Eph 5:15
See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise,
Gal 5:16
This I say then, Walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh.
Mic 6:8
He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
Furthermore then we beseech you, brethren, and exhort you by the Lord Jesus, that as ye have received of us how ye ought to walk and to please God, so ye would abound more and more.
corruption_summary: His Daily Walk answered what a justified man does between breakfast and bed, and was read for two centuries.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a pair. One is the self-improvement manual with a Christian veneer, which hands the reader techniques and never mentions the cross, so that holiness becomes a project of the self. The other is the doctrinal preaching that stops short of Tuesday morning and leaves the hearer agreeing with everything and changing nothing. Scudder avoided both by assuming the gospel and then being extremely specific.

The principle to recover is that Scripture itself is specific about the walk. “See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise” (Eph 5:15). The power is not the walker's own: “Walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh” (Gal 5:16). The whole requirement can be said in a line — “to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God” (Mic 6:8) — and the apostolic exhortation is to go on improving at it: “as ye have received of us how ye ought to walk and to please God, so ye would abound more and more” (1Th 4:1).

Greek akribos (G199) — exactly, accurately, circumspectly; Ephesians 5:15.
Greek epithumia (G1939) — desire, lust, craving; Galatians 5:16.
Hebrew tsana (H6800) — to be humble, to walk humbly; Micah 6:8.
Greek perisseuo (G4052) — to abound, to increase; 1 Thessalonians 4:1.

“Walk in the Spirit” (Gal 5:16) — practical divinity that assumes the gospel.
“so ye would abound more and more” (1Th 4:1) — commended by Owen and by Baxter.

pos: n. (Richard Byfield, c. 1598–1664, Westminster divine and defender of the sabbath)
etymology: Germanic Ricohard, strong in rule; English Byfield, dweller by the field.
biblical_def: Richard Byfield was rector of Long Ditton in Surrey, a member of the Westminster Assembly, and the author of a long vindication of the Lord's Day against those who held the fourth commandment wholly ceremonial and the Christian Sunday a matter of church custom only. He was ejected in 1662. His case was the ordinary Puritan one: that the commandment to keep one day in seven holy belongs to the moral law and binds all men, that the particular day was changed by apostolic authority to the first of the week in honour of the resurrection, and that the day is for worship, rest and mercy rather than for sport or trade. The dictionary holds that position. It also notes what the sabbath is for, since the word has acquired in modern use a reputation for severity which the fourth commandment does not have: the day is a gift of rest to a working people, and it is the only commandment that explicitly protects the servant and the stranger.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sabbath as a day of rest set apart for religious duties, and moral law as the law of God prescribing moral duties.
webster_full: SAB'BATH, n. The day which God appointed to be observed by the Jews as a day of rest; among Christians, the first day of the week, in commemoration of our Saviour's resurrection.
MOR'AL, a. Relating to the practice, manners or conduct of men as social beings; as the moral law.
CEREMO'NIAL, a. Relating to ceremony or external rite; ritual.
VINDICA'TION, n. The act of vindicating; defense; justification against denial or censure.
scriptures: Exo 20:8
Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy.

If thou turn away thy foot from the sabbath, from doing thy pleasure on my holy day; and call the sabbath a delight, the holy of the LORD, honourable; and shalt honour him, not doing thine own ways, nor finding thine own pleasure, nor speaking thine own words:
Mar 2:27
And he said unto them, The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath:
Heb 4:9
There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God.
corruption_summary: He vindicated the Lord's Day as moral law, and the day itself as rest and mercy rather than severity.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse cuts both ways. In one direction the fourth commandment is dismissed as a ceremony abolished in Christ, with the result that a Christian people works and trades seven days and wonders why it is exhausted. In the other, sabbath keeping becomes a competition in abstentions, and the day that was given for rest and mercy is made a burden — which our Lord addressed directly in the Gospels.

The principle to recover is that the day is commanded, is holy, and is a gift. “Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy” (Exo 20:8). It is to be a pleasure and not a privation: “call the sabbath a delight, the holy of the LORD, honourable” (Isa 58:13). Its direction is settled by Christ Himself: “The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath” (Mar 2:27). And it points beyond itself — “There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God” (Heb 4:9).

pos: n. (John White of Dorchester, 1575–1648, Puritan rector and promoter of the Massachusetts settlement)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan through Latin Johannes, the LORD is gracious; English White, of fair complexion.
biblical_def: John White was rector of Holy Trinity, Dorchester, for forty years, and he reordered the town around the gospel: a brewhouse whose profits funded poor relief, a municipal hospital for the children of the poor, a free school, and a strict corporate discipline, after a fire in 1613 which he preached as a judgment and used as an occasion. He was also the chief promoter of the Dorchester Company that settled Cape Ann, and so a founder of the plantation that became Massachusetts; he never crossed the Atlantic himself. The dictionary names him because of the combination. White's interest in the colony was not commercial and not escapist: he wanted a church in New England and a reformed town in old England, and he put the same money and preaching into both. A reformation that cannot show itself in how a parish treats its poor has not reached the ground.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines plantation as a colony or original settlement, and relief as the removal of any evil that afflicts the body.
webster_full: PLANTA'TION, n. The act of planting or setting in the earth; a colony; an original settlement in a new country.
RELIE'F, n. The removal, in whole or in part, of any evil that afflicts the body or mind; succour.
CORPORA'TION, n. A body politic or corporate, formed and authorized by law.
HOS'PITAL, n. A building appropriated for the reception of sick, infirm and helpless paupers.
scriptures: Jam 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
Isa 1:17
Learn to do well; seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow.
Pro 31:9
Open thy mouth, judge righteously, and plead the cause of the poor and needy.
Jer 29:5
Build ye houses, and dwell in them; and plant gardens, and eat the fruit of them;
corruption_summary: He reformed Dorchester's care of its poor and promoted the plantation that became Massachusetts.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern division of labour by which the gospel is preached by one set of people and the poor are relieved by another, usually the state, with the result that a congregation may hold sound doctrine and have no idea what is happening in the next street. White preached, and he also built a hospital and a school and found work for the unemployed, and he did not regard the second as an addition to his ministry.

The principle to recover is that God defines pure religion in terms that include the fatherless and the widow. “Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world” (Jam 1:27). The prophetic charge is concrete: “relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow” (Isa 1:17). Speech is required of those with standing: “plead the cause of the poor and needy” (Pro 31:9). And a people planting in a new place is told to build, dwell and plant — “Build ye houses, and dwell in them; and plant gardens, and eat the fruit of them” (Jer 29:5).

“Build ye houses, and dwell in them” (Jer 29:5) — the Dorchester Company and Cape Ann.

pos: n. (Stanley Gower, d. 1660, Westminster divine, chaplain to the Harleys and preacher before Parliament)
etymology: English Stanley, the stony clearing; Welsh Gower, from the Gower peninsula.
biblical_def: Stanley Gower was trained in Ireland under the ministry of the Scottish and English preachers of the Ulster plantation, became chaplain to Sir Robert Harley at Brampton Bryan in Herefordshire, and from there to the rectory of Dorchester and a seat in the Westminster Assembly. He preached before the House of Commons in 1644 on the duty of rulers, and he edited the papers of the Irish preacher Robert Blair's circle. The dictionary names him for the sermon before Parliament and for what such sermons were. The Assembly's divines were regularly called to preach to the men who had the power of the sword, and they used the occasion to tell them their duty from Scripture rather than to flatter them — which is the whole point of having a preacher who is not on the payroll of the party he is addressing. That relationship between pulpit and power is as hard to keep now as it was then, and in both directions.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines chaplain as a clergyman who officiates in a family or a court, and fast-sermon as a discourse preached on a day of public humiliation.
webster_full: CHAP'LAIN, n. An ecclesiastic who has the care of a chapel; a clergyman who belongs to a court, a regiment or a family.
HUMILIA'TION, n. The act of humbling; a day appointed for public fasting and prayer.
PAR'LIAMENT, n. The grand assembly of the three estates, the supreme legislature of Great Britain.
REC'TOR, n. A clergyman who has the charge and cure of a parish.
scriptures: The God of Israel said, the Rock of Israel spake to me, He that ruleth over men must be just, ruling in the fear of God.
Psa 2:10
Be wise now therefore, O ye kings: be instructed, ye judges of the earth.
Righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people.
And as he reasoned of righteousness, temperance, and judgment to come, Felix trembled, and answered, Go thy way for this time; when I have a convenient season, I will call for thee.
corruption_summary: He preached to the House of Commons on the duty of rulers rather than on the merits of their cause.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse runs two ways and both are familiar. A preacher with access to power may become its chaplain in the bad sense, supplying religious warrant for whatever his patrons have decided; or he may conclude that the pulpit has nothing to say to rulers at all, which leaves them with no word from God. Scripture gives the preacher something specific to say to a magistrate, and it is neither flattery nor silence.

The principle to recover is that rulers are addressed by God and told their duty. “He that ruleth over men must be just, ruling in the fear of God” (2Sa 23:3). The psalm addresses them directly: “Be wise now therefore, O ye kings: be instructed, ye judges of the earth” (Psa 2:10). The standard applied to a nation is moral: “Righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people” (Pro 14:34). And the pattern of a preacher before a governor is Paul before Felix, reasoning “of righteousness, temperance, and judgment to come” (Act 24:25).
